name: Cyber Security
description: Threat modelling, authentication, common attacks, defence in depth and incident response.

modules.name: Principles & Threat Modelling
modules.description: How to think about security before you think about tools.

cards.prompt: What is the CIA triad?
cards.answer: Confidentiality (only authorised parties can read it), Integrity (data cannot be altered undetected), Availability (the system is usable when needed).
cards.explanation: Most controls trade between them: aggressive rate limiting protects integrity and availability but can deny legitimate users; heavy encryption protects confidentiality but complicates recovery. Naming which property you are protecting sharpens every design argument.

cards.prompt: What four questions does a threat model answer, and what does STRIDE add?
cards.answer: What are we building? What can go wrong? What are we going to do about it? Did we do a good job? STRIDE enumerates threat categories: Spoofing, Tampering, Repudiation, Information disclosure, Denial of service, Elevation of privilege.
cards.explanation: Threat modelling is a whiteboard activity, not a tool purchase. Draw the data flows, mark the trust boundaries, and walk STRIDE at each boundary. Most exploitable design flaws are visible at that diagram stage.

cards.prompt: Name the core security design principles.
cards.answer: Least privilege, defence in depth, fail securely, complete mediation, separation of duties, minimise the attack surface, no security through obscurity, and secure defaults.
cards.explanation: Least privilege and secure defaults do most of the work in practice. 'Fail securely' is the one people get backwards: an auth service timing out must deny, not allow — that error path is where real breaches happen.

cards.prompt: What does zero trust actually change compared with a perimeter model?
cards.answer: It stops treating network location as authorisation. Every request is authenticated and authorised on its own merits — strong identity for users *and* services, device posture checks, and per-request policy rather than 'inside the VPN is trusted'.
cards.explanation: The perimeter model fails on the first compromised laptop: the attacker inherits everything the network trusts. In practice zero trust means mTLS between services, short-lived credentials, and authorisation decisions at each hop.

modules.name: Attacks & Defences
modules.description: The attacks you will actually meet, and the controls that stop them.

cards.prompt: Authentication vs authorisation
cards.answer: Authentication proves who you are; authorisation decides what you may do.

right.title: Authorisation (AuthZ)
points: Checked on every request and object

cards.explanation: Broken access control is the number one item in the OWASP Top 10 — usually because authorisation was checked in the UI or at the route, but not on the object. Every handler must verify that *this* user may touch *this* record.

cards.prompt: What is wrong with this password storage?
cards.answer: SHA-256 is a fast general-purpose hash with no salt — perfect for GPU cracking at billions of guesses per second. Use a memory-hard password hash: Argon2id, scrypt or bcrypt, each of which salts automatically.
cards.explanation: Password hashing must be *deliberately slow and memory-hungry* so an attacker with the dump cannot brute-force it. Argon2id is the current recommendation; tune the parameters so verification takes tens of milliseconds on your hardware.

cards.prompt: What are the three kinds of XSS, and what actually stops them?
cards.answer: Stored (payload persisted server-side), reflected (payload echoed from the request) and DOM-based (client-side sink such as `innerHTML`). The defence is context-aware output encoding, plus avoiding dangerous sinks — with CSP as the backstop.
cards.explanation: Encoding must match the context: HTML body, attribute, JavaScript string and URL each escape differently. Modern frameworks escape by default, so most real XSS now comes from deliberately unsafe escapes (`dangerouslySetInnerHTML`, `v-html`) or from `href="javascript:"`.

cards.prompt: How does CSRF work, and what stops it today?
cards.answer: An attacker's page triggers a state-changing request to your site; the browser attaches the victim's cookies automatically. Defences: `SameSite=Lax/Strict` cookies, anti-CSRF tokens, and requiring a custom header that cross-origin forms cannot set.
cards.explanation: CSRF exploits ambient authority — the browser sending credentials without the page proving it meant to. Token-based auth in an `Authorization` header is naturally immune, because nothing attaches it automatically.

cards.prompt: Why is this endpoint dangerous in a cloud environment?
cards.answer: Server-side request forgery. An attacker can point it at internal services or the cloud metadata endpoint (169.254.169.254) and retrieve credentials. Validate against an allowlist, block private and link-local ranges, and re-check after redirects.
cards.explanation: SSRF caused the Capital One breach. DNS rebinding and redirects defeat naive checks, so resolve the hostname, validate the resulting IP, and connect to that IP. Enforcing IMDSv2 removes the easiest credential-theft path on AWS.

cards.prompt: A secret was committed to a public repository. What do you do?
cards.answer: Rotate it immediately — assume it is compromised the moment it lands. Removing the commit is secondary: it was cloned, cached and scraped within minutes. Then add scanning to prevent recurrence.
cards.explanation: Git history rewriting does not un-publish anything. Prevention: pre-commit secret scanning, `.gitignore` for env files, and a secret manager (Vault, AWS Secrets Manager, SOPS) so secrets never sit in the repo or in plain environment files.

resources.title: GitHub Docs — Removing sensitive data from a repository

cards.prompt: What are the phases of incident response?
cards.answer: Preparation, detection and analysis, containment, eradication, recovery, and post-incident review — with evidence preservation running through all of them.
cards.explanation: The instinct to 'clean up and move on' destroys the evidence needed to know what was taken. Snapshot before you wipe. The blameless post-mortem is where the actual value is: the same class of failure recurs until the system changes.

resources.title: NIST SP 800-61 — Computer Security Incident Handling Guide

modules.name: Identity, Sessions & Access
modules.description: MFA and passkeys, session management, brute-force defences, account enumeration and access-control models.

cards.prompt: SMS/TOTP codes vs passkeys (WebAuthn/FIDO2)
cards.answer: One-time codes add a second factor but can be phished — a fake site relays them in real time — and SMS is vulnerable to SIM swapping. Passkeys use public-key cryptography bound to the site's origin, so they cannot be phished or replayed and there is no shared secret to leak.

left.title: SMS / TOTP codes
points: Shared secret or code sent to the user
Phishable: codes can be relayed live

right.title: Passkeys / FIDO2
points: Per-site key pair; private key stays on device
Nothing reusable to steal from the server

cards.explanation: Any MFA beats none: it stops credential stuffing cold. For high-value accounts prefer phishing-resistant factors — passkeys or hardware security keys. Plan account recovery carefully; weak recovery flows are where attackers go once MFA is strong.

cards.prompt: What are the rules for secure session management?
cards.answer: Generate long random session IDs with a CSPRNG; store them in `HttpOnly; Secure; SameSite` cookies; rotate the ID at login and privilege change (prevents session fixation); expire on idle and absolute timeouts; invalidate server-side on logout and password change.
cards.explanation: Never put session IDs in URLs — they leak through logs, history and the Referer header. Offer "log out everywhere", and for sensitive actions re-authenticate rather than trusting an old session.

cards.prompt: Your login endpoint is hit by credential stuffing from thousands of IPs. What defences work?
cards.answer: MFA (the strongest single control), rate limits per account and per IP with growing delays, checking passwords against breached-password lists (e.g. Have I Been Pwned's k-anonymity API), bot detection or CAPTCHAs after failures, and alerting on anomalous login volume.
cards.explanation: Hard account lockout lets an attacker lock out every user on purpose, so prefer throttling and step-up challenges. Per-IP limits alone fail against botnets with residential proxies, which is why per-account signals matter.

resources.title: OWASP Cheat Sheet — Credential Stuffing Prevention

cards.prompt: What does this login response leak?
cards.answer: Distinct messages tell an attacker which emails have accounts, letting them build a target list for phishing and credential stuffing. Return the same generic message ("invalid email or password") and similar response times for both cases — and apply the same to sign-up and password reset.
cards.explanation: Timing leaks too: skipping the password hash for unknown users makes their responses measurably faster. Hash against a dummy value so both paths cost the same.

resources.title: OWASP Cheat Sheet — Authentication — Authentication and error messages

cards.prompt: What are RBAC, ABAC and ReBAC?
cards.answer: Role-based: permissions attach to roles (admin, editor) assigned to users. Attribute-based: policies evaluate attributes of user, resource and context ("managers may approve expenses in their department under £5,000 during business hours"). Relationship-based: access follows relationships in a graph ("viewers of a folder can view its documents"), as in Google Zanzibar.
cards.explanation: RBAC is simplest and suits most apps until role explosion sets in. Document-sharing products tend towards ReBAC; regulated environments towards ABAC. Whatever the model, centralise the decision in one policy layer and check it on every object access.

modules.name: Threats, Vulnerabilities & Resilience
modules.description: Attack frameworks, vulnerability management, testing approaches, phishing, ransomware and backups, DDoS, segmentation and risk.

cards.prompt: What is MITRE ATT&CK, and how does it relate to the cyber kill chain?
cards.answer: The kill chain describes an intrusion as stages — reconnaissance, weaponisation, delivery, exploitation, installation, command and control, actions on objectives. MITRE ATT&CK is a detailed, evidence-based catalogue of real attacker tactics and techniques (initial access, persistence, privilege escalation, lateral movement, exfiltration…).
cards.explanation: Defenders use ATT&CK to map which techniques they can detect and where the gaps are. The key insight from both: attackers must succeed at every stage, so detection and disruption anywhere along the chain can stop them.

cards.prompt: What are CVE, CVSS, and why is CVSS score alone a poor way to prioritise patching?
cards.answer: A CVE is a unique identifier for a publicly known vulnerability; CVSS scores its technical severity from 0 to 10. But severity is not risk: exploitability in the wild (CISA's Known Exploited Vulnerabilities list, EPSS probability), your exposure, and the asset's value matter more.
cards.explanation: A 9.8 in an unreachable internal library may matter less than a 6.5 on your internet-facing login page being actively exploited. Keep an inventory (SBOMs help), patch known-exploited issues first, and track time-to-remediate as a metric.

cards.prompt: Penetration test vs red team exercise vs bug bounty
cards.answer: A pentest is a time-boxed assessment of a defined scope to find as many vulnerabilities as possible. A red team emulates a real adversary pursuing an objective, testing detection and response as much as prevention. A bug bounty invites continuous outside research, paying per valid finding.

right.title: Red team / bug bounty
points: Red team: tests detection and response
Bounty: pay per valid, in-scope finding

cards.explanation: Order matters: fix the basics and run pentests before paying bounties, or you pay repeatedly for easy bugs. Red teaming only makes sense once you have detection and response capability worth testing.

cards.prompt: An employee receives an urgent email from the "CEO" asking for a wire transfer. What controls stop business email compromise?
cards.answer: Process controls: out-of-band verification (call a known number) for payment or bank-detail changes, and dual approval above a threshold. Technical controls: SPF, DKIM and DMARC at `p=reject` against domain spoofing, external-sender banners, and lookalike-domain monitoring. Plus training that makes reporting easy and blame-free.
cards.explanation: Social engineering targets people and processes, so purely technical defences are not enough. Urgency, authority and secrecy are the signature tactics. The strongest control is a rule that bank details never change on the strength of an email alone.

resources.title: CISA — Avoiding social engineering and phishing attacks

cards.prompt: What backup strategy survives ransomware?
cards.answer: The 3-2-1 rule — three copies, on two kinds of media, one off-site — extended with one immutable or offline copy (object lock, WORM storage, credentials separate from production) and regular restore tests. Ransomware operators deliberately find and delete reachable backups first.
cards.explanation: If the same admin account can delete production and backups, one compromised credential ends both. Measure recovery time with drills, and keep backups long enough to predate a slow, quiet intrusion.

cards.prompt: What kinds of DDoS attacks are there, and how are they mitigated?
cards.answer: Volumetric floods (saturate bandwidth, often via amplification — DNS, NTP, memcached reflection), protocol attacks (SYN floods exhausting connection state), and application-layer attacks (expensive HTTP requests that look legitimate). Mitigation: upstream scrubbing and anycast CDNs, SYN cookies, rate limiting, caching, and autoscaling with cost limits.
cards.explanation: Application-layer floods are the hardest because each request looks normal — make expensive endpoints cheap or authenticated, and cache aggressively. You cannot out-bandwidth a large botnet from one data centre; that is what DDoS-protection providers exist for.

resources.title: Cloudflare Learning — What is a DDoS attack?

cards.prompt: Why segment a network, and what does lateral movement mean?
cards.answer: Lateral movement is an attacker pivoting from the first compromised machine to others. Segmentation splits the network into zones with controlled paths between them — production away from corporate laptops, databases reachable only from their applications — so one foothold does not reach everything.
cards.explanation: Flat networks turn a phished laptop into a domain-wide breach. Micro-segmentation extends the idea per workload with identity-based policies, which is where it meets zero trust. Watch east–west traffic, not only the perimeter.

cards.prompt: How is security risk assessed, and what are the ways to treat a risk?
cards.answer: Risk ≈ likelihood × impact, judged for each threat against each asset. Treatments: mitigate (add controls), transfer (insurance, contracts), avoid (stop doing the risky thing), or accept (explicitly, by someone with the authority to).
cards.explanation: Security cannot remove all risk, so the job is prioritisation: spend effort where likelihood and impact are highest. A risk register with named owners turns vague worry into decisions that can be revisited.

cards.prompt: What are the core data-protection principles engineers should design for (as in GDPR)?
cards.answer: Lawful basis and purpose limitation (collect for a stated purpose, use only for that), data minimisation, accuracy, storage limitation (delete when no longer needed), integrity and confidentiality, and accountability. Users have rights to access, correct, export and erase their data.
cards.explanation: Privacy by design turns these into engineering: collect fewer fields, set retention and deletion jobs from day one, pseudonymise analytics, keep personal data out of logs, and know where every copy lives — backups, caches and third-party processors included — so erasure is possible.
